notes.meaning: The angel who had been talking with Zechariah woke him up, like someone being shaken awake from sleep. Zechariah was exhausted and overwhelmed by the amazing visions he had already seen. God revived the prophet's attention so he could receive another divine message.

Zechariah sees a solid gold lampstand with a bowl on top and seven lamps, fed by pipes. In the old tabernacle, priests had to keep refilling the lamps by hand, but this lampstand had an abundant, continuous supply of oil. The lampstand represents God's people shining His light into a dark world.

Two olive trees stand right beside the bowl, one on each side. They supply fresh olive oil directly into the bowl without any human help. This picture shows that God provides the grace and power His church needs to keep burning bright.

Zechariah respectfully asks the angel to explain what he is looking at. Although he can see the lampstand and trees, he knows they carry a deeper spiritual meaning. God welcomes humble questions from those who want to understand His truth.

The angel asks Zechariah if he knows what these objects mean, and the prophet honestly admits that he does not. The angel's question is meant to stir Zechariah's thoughts and prepare him to listen carefully. God readily teaches people who acknowledge their own lack of wisdom.

God sends an encouraging message to Zerubbabel, the governor rebuilding the ruined temple in Jerusalem. The great task will not succeed through large armies or human strength, but by God's Holy Spirit. Just as the lamps were fed by living trees without human hands, God's work is completed by His own quiet power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some interpreters note that it is premature to read 'Spirit' here as the fully revealed third Person of the Trinity, though the passage prepares the way for that truth.

notes.meaning: The enormous obstacles facing Zerubbabel are compared to a high, impassable mountain. God promises that this mountain of trouble will be flattened out like level ground. Zerubbabel will successfully set the final capstone in place while the people shout praises for God's free grace and favor.

The Lord promises that because Zerubbabel laid the temple's foundation, he will live to complete the building. When the work is finished, the people will know for certain that God truly sent His messenger. Finishing the earthly house also gives proof that God will bring His spiritual kingdom to completion.

The people are warned not to look down on the rebuilding project just because its start was small and weak. The Lord's all-seeing eyes watch over the whole earth, and He rejoices to see Zerubbabel holding the plumb line to finish the walls. God often takes humble beginnings and turns them into great victories.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older commentators suggest the seven eyes can represent the seven chief angels who watch over the earth under God's providence.

notes.meaning: Zechariah asks the angel again about the two olive trees standing on the left and right sides of the lampstand. He wants to know who or what these living sources of oil represent. Those who want to grow in God's wisdom keep asking until they understand His message.

Zechariah looks closer and asks about the two olive branches that pour golden oil through two golden pipes into the bowl. The rich oil flows out constantly from the branches like liquid gold. This portrays the unending supply of spiritual life and grace that God pours out upon His people.

Once again, the angel asks Zechariah if he understands what the branches are, and the prophet humbly replies that he does not. The angel brings out this confession of ignorance so the prophet will pay close attention to the final answer. God reveals His deep truths to those who are lowly and teachable.

The angel reveals that the branches represent the two anointed servants who stand before the Lord of all the earth. In Zechariah's day, these were Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor, whom God filled with His Spirit to lead the church and the nation. In a greater way, they point forward to Christ, who serves as both King and Priest for His people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: A traditional interpretation identifies these two figures with Enoch and Elijah, connecting them to the two prophetic witnesses described in Revelation.
